evaluation.positioning_hook: A sober ex-soldier turned homeless bodyguard saves a Glasgow crime boss from an ambush, then leverages the rescue into a job that drags him back into the violence he’s trying to outrun.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is clean and the lead is built for a hard-edged adult audience, but the appeal is narrower than a broad four-quadrant crime title. The Scottish setting, addiction angle, and criminal underworld give it a defined lane rather than a mass-market one.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The opening ambush, five-years-later sobriety reset, and Roddy Kincaid recruitment path make the premise easy to grasp in two sentences. The script lands its engine early, even if the larger endgame is still more setup than payoff in this excerpt.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Knox has a strong contradiction set: disciplined protector, alcoholic in recovery, homeless, and still dangerous when cornered. Kincaid is also vivid, with charm, menace, and a need for competent help, though the supporting cast is thinner than the lead.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The material has a distinct voice through the Scottish dialogue, the AA-to-underworld pivot, and the hard-boiled humor. The underlying crime-boss-recruits-protector setup is familiar, though the specific social texture helps it stand apart.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves quickly from ambush to recovery to recruitment, and the assassination attempt in the alley gives it a strong jolt. As a feature opening, though, it reads more like a launch pad than a fully escalating story engine.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The combination of a homeless ex-operator, AA meetings, and a Glasgow crime outfit creates a fresh enough collision to feel ownable. It is immediately legible why this works: a damaged man with elite skills is pulled back into a world that values exactly what he is trying to bury.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The script has a lived-in Scottish criminal ecosystem: gym, nightclub office, church confessional, AA hall, and street-level violence all feel connected. The dialect, class texture, and side characters like Maureen and Kincaid’s crew give the world story-generating specificity.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is sharply regional, profane, and darkly comic, with a strong undercurrent of bruised masculinity. The script knows how to pivot from absurdity in the AA room to sudden violence in the car park and alley.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Knox’s PTSD, sobriety, and relationship to his son suggest deeper emotional material beneath the crime plot. In this excerpt, that depth is present but still mostly implied through behavior rather than fully dramatized.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Knox and Kincaid have a strong lead-partner friction dynamic, and the crew around them has usable texture. Still, most supporting characters function as orbiting pieces around Knox rather than as a fully generative ensemble system.

lead_characters.name: Jack Knox
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, Scottish, ex-military, recovering alcoholic, formerly homeless.
lead_characters.hook: A hard-bitten former close-protection man with PTSD, Knox is introduced shaking in a hotel bathroom, then revealed as a resourceful survivor who has fallen all the way to the street. He’s funny, defensive, and deeply self-aware without ever sounding sentimental; the script keeps him in constant contradiction between discipline and collapse, shame and competence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a Michael Keaton in Birdman or a Matthew McConaughey in True Detective-style turn: a damaged man whose intelligence, menace, and vulnerability all live in the same frame. The role gives an actor the chance to play physical authority, dry comic timing, and emotional wreckage without ever leaving the crime-thriller lane.

lead_characters.name: Roddy Kincaid
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, Scottish, crime boss / nightclub operator.
lead_characters.hook: Kincaid is a polished, volatile operator who talks like a philosopher and threatens like a gangster. He’s vain, strategic, and insecure about loyalty, which makes him both dangerous and oddly readable; he wants control, but he also wants someone competent enough to trust.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the same juice as Mark Strong in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy or Ray Winstone in Sexy Beast: controlled menace with flashes of wit and wounded pride. It’s a scene-stealing part for an actor who can make charm feel like a weapon.

lead_characters.name: Paul McKissack
lead_characters.hook: McKissack is Knox’s working partner in the opening ambush, a competent bodyguard whose injury and near-death establish the stakes before the story jumps ahead. He’s not yet deeply individualized, but he functions as the emotional evidence of Knox’s old life and the cost of the job.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is solid character-actor territory in the vein of a Stephen Graham supporting turn: efficient, grounded, and memorable in a few scenes. It offers a performer the chance to make a small role feel lived-in and dangerous.

lead_characters.name: Sloane Kincaid
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s-30s, Scottish, Roddy Kincaid’s daughter, office/accounting role.
lead_characters.hook: Sloane is introduced as the sharp-eyed daughter doing the books, and she immediately reads Knox with skepticism rather than deference. She suggests a quieter intelligence inside the criminal family structure, and she has enough edge to feel like a future pressure point.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that can do for an actor what Juno Temple got in Fargo or what a strong supporting daughter role does in a crime family piece: intelligence, attitude, and the ability to shift a room without raising her voice. It’s a clean showcase for controlled authority.

lead_characters.name: Maureen
lead_characters.demographics: Female, middle-aged to older, Scottish, AA meeting attendee.
lead_characters.hook: Maureen is a comic-tragic AA presence whose monologue spirals from addiction to family catastrophe to domestic absurdity. She’s written as a vivid local voice, and the scene gives the script a human, street-level texture that broadens the world beyond the crime plot.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a character-actor gift in the vein of a Shirley Henderson or Olivia Colman supporting scene: a single speech that can land comedy, pain, and specificity at once. It gives an actor a memorable, audience-leaning moment without needing a huge page count.

lead_characters.name: Rab
lead_characters.demographics: Male, middle-aged, Scottish, gym owner under financial pressure.
lead_characters.hook: Rab is the struggling gym owner whose debt crisis helps pull Knox back into the orbit of the criminal world. He’s a practical, beaten-down operator rather than a flashy gangster, which makes the financial stakes feel grounded and local.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that suits a veteran character actor who can play exhaustion and pride at the same time, like Peter Mullan in a supporting turn. It’s a believable, textured part that adds weight to the world.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Knox is a star-making antihero role.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project a casting hook that can open doors with actors who want a bruised, funny, physically credible lead role. Buyers chasing elevated crime material will see a part that can anchor the whole film even on a modest budget.
strengths.evidence: The hotel-bathroom ritual, the AA meeting, the alleyway save, and the dry one-liners all build a man who is both broken and dangerous.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Scottish crime world feels lived-in.
strengths.what_it_means: A specific regional texture makes the script easier to position than a generic gangster piece and gives it a clearer identity in a crowded market. That specificity is attractive to buyers who want local flavor with exportable genre mechanics.
strengths.evidence: The AA room, the gym, the church confessional, and the nightclub office all carry the same dialect, class, and social rhythm.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The opening ambush is a strong cold-start engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The script announces stakes immediately and gives a producer a clean trailer moment to sell. It also establishes the competence of the lead before the story time-jumps, which is useful for audience trust.
strengths.evidence: The hotel car-park attack, Knox’s gun safety mistake, and McKissack’s injury create instant danger and confusion.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The dialogue has a sharp comic bite.
strengths.what_it_means: That voice gives the material a marketable tonal edge and helps it stand out from more generic grim crime scripts. It also broadens the casting appeal because performers get to play wit, not just menace.
strengths.evidence: The AA meeting, the confessional exchange, and Knox’s banter with Kincaid all land as profane, specific, and character-revealing.

strengths.what_it_means: A contemporary, location-light crime feature is easier to finance and package than a larger action title, especially when the lead role is the main selling point. That makes it viable for indie financiers and streamer genre teams alike.
strengths.evidence: Most scenes are interiors or controlled exteriors, with only one major ambush and one alley fight carrying action scope.

The combination of bruised antihero drama and modest indie scale makes it the kind of package that can get traction with both character-actor talent and genre buyers.

Beyond that, the project is highly dependent on the lead performance and on whether the full script expands the supporting world beyond Knox and Kincaid.
